title: A pricing page for a two-sided marketplace
excerpt: The side you need first uses pricing to judge fit. Show what the fee includes, what it does not, and the shape of the price they will ask for anyway.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, like a pricing page that asks one side to judge the road ahead.
caption: A long road with one car and a clear destination. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a marketplace pricing page show first?
faqs.answer: Show the fee the scarce side will actually pay or forfeit, including who is charged and when. Put that shape near the top, with a short list of what it includes and what it does not. The other side can have a clearly marked block of its own, after the side you need first can judge fit.

faqs.question: What if every job has a different price?
faqs.answer: Publish the shape even when the final number moves. A percentage, a rate card, or one realistic worked example is enough for a fit decision. If a quote is required, say which facts you need and when a number comes back. A button that only says the price is custom does not answer the question they arrived with.

faqs.question: Should marketplace pricing be hidden until a sales call?
faqs.answer: Hide a number only when the offer truly cannot be stated in public, and still describe the smallest and largest work you will take. A simple take rate does not need a meeting. Visitors who will ask the price anyway should see the shape on the page, then a join path that tells them what happens next.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The two-sided marketplace pricing page is where the side you need first decides whether joining fits. They are judging the deal, and they are not ready to do arithmetic. Show what the fee includes, what it leaves out, and how that side joins. If they will ask the price anyway, say the shape on the page.

A table of tiers can still be the right layout. It fails when every row is a slogan and the fee appears only after a call the visitor did not come to book. Fit is a yes or no. The math can wait until they trust the yes.

## Judge fit before the spreadsheet

The scarce side arrives with a private calculation already in mind. A coach knows what a session is worth in their city. A host knows what a Saturday night covers in food and time. A carrier knows the floor under which a lane is a favor, not a job. Your page does not need their spreadsheet. It needs to give them the inputs they cannot guess.

Those inputs are the fee, who pays it, when it is charged, and what they receive before they have earned a dollar. A percentage with no base is a riddle. "15%" of what, taken when, from which side? Say "15% of the completed booking, taken from the host payout, after the dinner runs." A visitor can reject that in one reading. Rejection is a successful page if the alternative was a week of mismatched sales calls.

Nielsen Norman Group found that people have time to read only about a quarter of the text on the pages they actually visit. On a pricing page, that quarter will be whatever sits nearest the fee. Put the shape there. A paragraph of philosophy above the number will be the paragraph they skip, or the only paragraph they see, and neither outcome tells them the deal.

Write the first screen as a single offer for the side you need. If the other side also pays, give them a second block with a heading in their words, below the fold or on a tab they can open. Do not interleave the two fees in one grid and hope the labels sort it out.

## Say what the fee includes

"Included" is a list of work, not a list of adjectives. For the side joining first, name the things the fee actually buys.

A listing that stays up. A payout to a bank account on a stated schedule. A review that the other side can see. Dispute handling up to a defined point. Email support, or a named human, during named hours. Verification you perform, such as a license check, and verification you do not.

Each line should be something a person could notice missing. "Access to the platform" is not that line. They already assumed access when they considered joining. "Payouts every Friday for jobs completed by Wednesday" is a line they can plan around.

If the early period is subsidized, say the subsidy as a date or a count. "No fee on your first three completed jobs" is a fit signal. "Introductory pricing" is a postponement. The careful visitor hears a change they cannot see coming, and they wait, or they leave.

Keep the list short enough to compare with the other places they could sell the same work. A coach comparing you with a direct booking link needs three or four lines, not a feature matrix copied from a software category page.

## Say what the fee does not include

The exclusions are where trust is won or lost. The side you need first has been surprised before. They want the surprise written down.

Name the costs that sit outside the fee. Payment processing. Chargebacks. Refunds you claw back. Taxes they still remit. Equipment, ingredients, fuel, insurance they must carry themselves. A premium placement they can buy later. A city you do not serve.

Say who eats a cancellation. If the guest cancels inside two hours and the host keeps the fee, write that. If the host cancels and the guest is refunded while the host owes nothing, write that too. Ambiguity here reads as "we will decide later, in our favor."

Google's guidance on title links is a small, useful constraint on this page. The title should say that the page is about price, in words a stranger would use, and it should be distinct from the homepage title. "Pricing" is enough when the brand is already in the title pattern. "Flexible plans for growing ecosystems" could sit on any company, and it tells search results nothing a visitor can use. The same test applies to the headings on the page. "Simple" is not an exclusion, and it is not an inclusion.

Read the exclusions as if you were the scarce side's accountant. If a line would make that person write back "but what about refunds," the line is not finished.

## Show the shape when the number moves

Some markets cannot print one number. Freight varies by lane. Care varies by hours and credentials. Local services vary by city. Hiding the entire price behind "contact sales" still fails, because the visitor will ask anyway, and they asked on this visit.

Show the shape. A percentage. A monthly seat plus a per-job fee. A range you have actually charged, labeled as a range. A worked example with the units they use: one dinner for eight, one 200-mile run, one four-hour shift. The example can say "illustrative" if the live price is calculated. It should still use a realistic figure, not a flattering one.

If a quote is required, say what the quote needs and when it comes back. "Origin, destination, ready date, and weight. A number the same day if you write before 2pm." That is a price shape. "Custom, talk to us" is a closed door with a nicer label.

Do not invent precision you do not have. A calculator that asks for twelve inputs and then says "we'll be in touch" has cost the visitor time and returned no fit judgment. Either the calculator produces a range you will honor, or it does not belong on the page.

The join path sits under the example, with the same label you use on the homepage. They came from a match. They should not have to relearn what joining is called.

## Keep the other side from taking the page

The side that pays the bill often wants the pricing page to face them. They are louder in meetings because they are the revenue line in the model. The seeding problem has not changed. If coaches will not list, athletes have nothing to buy, and a beautiful consumer price is a menu for an empty room.

Lead with the fee the scarce side pays, or the fee taken from them. Then show what the other side pays, in a clearly marked block. A family looking at care prices should not have to decode a worker's subscription to learn the hourly rate. A worker should not have to decode a family's membership to learn the take rate.

If the two prices are truly one price, say so once. "Families pay $35 an hour. Workers receive $28. The difference is the fee." That sentence is the whole model. Do not stretch it into three tiers with names like Sprout, Grove, and Canopy.

Tiers are justified when the work inside them is different. A free listing with a higher take rate, against a subscription with a lower one, is a real choice. Three tiers that differ by a checkmark on "analytics" are a software habit. The scarce side is not shopping for analytics. They are shopping for a market that will send them work.

## Put the join path where the decision happens

The pricing page is a decision page, so the action belongs next to the decision. Repeat it after the inclusions and after the worked example. One path, the same words, for the side you need first.

Tell them what the click asks for. "Apply as a host. You'll need a kitchen address, a menu, and a payout account. We reply within two business days." The number of days has to be a number you keep. A promise you miss becomes the story they tell the next host.

If some applicants are refused, say the basis in plain language. City, credentials, capacity, a kitchen inspection. Mystery rejection is a tax on the people you most want, because they have other places to sell their time.

The other side's action can be present as a secondary link. "Booking as a guest starts here." It should not be the button that shares color and size with the join path. You already made that mistake if the homepage has two equal buttons. Do not repeat it on the page where money is discussed.

## When a sales conversation is the honest next step

Some offers are too variable for a public number, and a conversation is the real product. Enterprise contracts, unusual compliance, a city you have never served. In that case the page still owes a shape: the smallest engagement you will take, the largest you will not, and what the conversation is for.

"We quote dedicated lanes above a minimum monthly volume. Below that, use the standard rate card." A visitor who is below the line can leave without a call, which saves both sides a meeting. A visitor who is above the line knows why they are booking time.

Do not use the conversation as a place to hide a simple percentage. If every customer pays 10%, the page can say 10%. A call to "walk through pricing" on a fee that fits in one sentence reads as reluctance. Reluctance reads as a worse number than the one you are avoiding.

The page that should sit next to this one explains the work itself, because a fee without a boundary still leaves the question of what you actually do. That is the [services page a two-sided marketplace actually needs](/blog/the-services-page-a-two-sided-marketplace-actually-needs).

For a look at how a public page can state one offer without a cloud of tiers, see [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works).
